note.text: Nationalism grew through interacting internal and external influences. Colonial land, labour, tax and racial inequalities produced grievances. Education, newspapers, religious and welfare associations, unions and towns helped people exchange ideas and organise. The war brought burdens and new experiences and weakened claims of European invincibility. Pan-African networks and examples of Asian independence encouraged activists; UN principles offered language and forums for claims. None automatically produced independence: organisation, popular support, political choices and the authorities’ responses mattered.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to classify internal and external influences and explain how a grievance became organised pressure for political change. Builds on: the meaning of nationalism and Pan-African solidarity. Leads to: Cameroonian pressure groups and party formation.

sections.heading: Explain the history
sections.text: Nationalism grew through interacting internal and external influences. Colonial land, labour, tax and racial inequalities produced grievances. Education, newspapers, religious and welfare associations, unions and towns helped people exchange ideas and organise. The war brought burdens and new experiences and weakened claims of European invincibility. sections.heading: Follow the evidence and examples
sections.text: At Manchester in {1945}, the Pan-African Congress brought together activists calling for an end to colonial domination. India’s independence in {1947} supplied a powerful external example, not a law instantly freeing Africa. In Cameroon, workers’ organisation linked employment grievances with wider political networks. Wartime service could expose contradictions between fighting for freedom and experiencing colonial inequality. A factor’s classification depends on the question: overseas congresses are external influences, while local organising turns ideas into action.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Explain the mechanism: a grievance supplies an issue; communication spreads it; an organisation sustains demands; an external example strengthens expectations. Avoid simply listing factors without links. Not all educated people or veterans held the same views. Superpower rhetoric about colonialism was selective and tied to strategic interests, rather than a guarantee of African freedom.

cards.idea: Check a claim against the sequence, setting and limits of the evidence.
example: Local land grievances were events occurring only in distant foreign capitals. Correction: These grievances arise within the society experiencing colonial rule.
A grievance automatically creates a durable organisation without communication. Correction: Networks help convert dissatisfaction into sustained collective action.
The Manchester Congress was a meeting confined to one Cameroonian plantation. Correction: Its international setting and participants made it a source of wider solidarity.
Indian independence legally granted every African territory immediate independence. Correction: An example can inspire activists without changing another territory’s legal status automatically.
